criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access, supply continuity, intermittence, pressure, and reliance on alternative water sources among households formally connected to the municipal distribution network in São Gonçalo, RJ.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading diverge. Under the broad/plain wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper passes (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include') because it frames unequal municipal/utility water allocation ('official water days' and socio-technical infrastructure prioritization), household metering/estimated-billing gaps, and the failure of official IBGE/SNIS connection indicators to capture intermittence as water-governance and institutional issues. Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is NOT met (c2_legal_admin_factor = 'no'): the study empirically compares water supply across two neighbourhoods stratified by socio-economic status (low-income Jardim Catarina vs. higher-income Mutondo) and attributes intermittent supply to socio-economic inequality ('hydrosocial scarcity') and physical storage-reservoir deficits rather than any rule-type legal, regulatory, eligibility, tenure/documentation, administrative-burden, tariff/cost-recovery, enforcement, or ownership mechanism governing access. Federal Laws 11,445/2007 and 14,026/2020 and the 2021 Águas do Rio concession appear only as unanalysed macro-governance background, descriptive survey items on absent meters and non-payment are reported as consequences/responses rather than a tested rule mechanism, and the authors explicitly note (p. 17) that deeper investigation of public policies and water service management lies beyond what is presented in the study.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from an in-situ comparative mixed-methods household survey conducted in November–December 2021 across two census tracts (n = 45 households in Jardim Catarina; n = 46 in Mutondo; total n = 91 semi-structured interviews).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete household-level service access outcomes including frequency of piped water delivery, intermittence/hours without water (up to 144 hours/week), water pressure, routine shortages, sufficiency for domestic needs, reliance on alternative sources and suction pumps, electricity cost burden, and perceived water security.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households/adult household heads in two census tracts, n = 91), the study's actual exposure/contrast (neighbourhood socio-economic status and uneven reservoir/distribution infrastructure), outcomes, and study design (comparative cross-sectional mixed-methods survey using typical-case sampling) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with Portuguese and Spanish abstracts).

study_design: Comparative cross-sectional mixed-methods household survey using non-probabilistic typical-case sampling of two contrasting census tracts
population_and_sample: Households formally connected to the municipal water network in two IBGE census tracts in São Gonçalo, Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region, Brazil: 45 households in Jardim Catarina (3rd District, Monjolos; 25% of 178 tract residences) and 46 households in Mutondo (1st District, São Gonçalo; 25% of 183 tract residences), total n = 91 adult household heads or spouses interviewed in November–December 2021
exposure: Neighbourhood socio-economic status (low-income Jardim Catarina vs. higher-income Mutondo) and incomplete physical water-storage reservoir infrastructure producing hydrosocial scarcity
outcome: Household piped water supply frequency and continuity, water pressure, routine water shortages, sufficiency for domestic needs, reliance on alternative water sources (wells, cisterns, water trucks, bottled water) and suction/hydraulic pumps, electricity cost burden, metering/payment rates, and perceived domestic water security
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although this empirical household survey (n = 91) examines piped drinking-water service continuity, pressure, shortages, and coping strategies in São Gonçalo, Brazil, its explanatory contrast is neighbourhood socio-economic status (low-income Jardim Catarina vs. higher-income Mutondo) alongside physical treated-water reservoir deficits ('hydrosocial scarcity'). It does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/disconnection enforcement rules, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Statutory references (Laws 11,445/2007 and 14,026/2020) and the 2021 concession to Águas do Rio serve only as unanalysed background, and the authors explicitly state that investigating public policies and water service management lies beyond the scope of the present study. Under the broad plain wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because institutional water rationing ('official water days'), metering/billing gaps, and official statistical invisibility are discussed within a water-governance framing.
